name: Mühle-Glashütte
tagline: Nautical instrument makers since 1869, building robust watches for rescuers and sailors
summary: Mühle-Glashütte is a family-run Glashütte company descended from Robert Mühle's 1869 precision-instrument workshop. Re-established in 1994, it makes marine chronometers and robust tool watches such as the S.A.R. Rescue-Timer, developed with the German Maritime Search and Rescue Service.
history:
Robert Mühle founded a precision-mechanics workshop in Glashütte on 22 April 1869, making measuring instruments for the town's growing watch industry. His sons joined the business, renamed R. Mühle & Sohn in 1905, and from 1918 it expanded into speedometers and car clocks.

After the Second World War the company was dismantled and absorbed into state enterprises. Hans Mühle re-established a small firm in December 1945, but in 1972 it too was expropriated and became part of the state-owned VEB Feinmechanik Glashütte. After reunification, Hans-Jürgen Mühle steered the business through privatisation and in 1994 re-founded the family company as Mühle-Glashütte GmbH nautische Instrumente und Feinmechanik, initially making marine chronometers, ship's clocks and nautical instruments.

The first Mühle wristwatches, a sports diver and the Marinefliegeruhr-I, went on sale in 1996. In 2002 the company delivered its first S.A.R. Rescue-Timers to the German Maritime Search and Rescue Service (DGzRS), and in 2003 it introduced its woodpecker neck regulation, a development of the swan-neck fine adjustment designed to keep the rate stable under shocks. Thilo Mühle took sole charge in 2007, and in 2011 the company presented the MU 9411, its first fully self-designed movement.

Today the family business, with the next generation joining management in 2024, offers robust tool watches for rescuers and sailors alongside accessible 29er sports watches and the classical Teutonia line.

name: MVMT
tagline: The crowdfunded, Instagram-built watch brand for millennials
summary: MVMT (pronounced 'movement') was founded in Los Angeles in 2013 by college dropouts Jake Kassan and Kramer LaPlante, who raised money on Indiegogo and sold minimalist watches directly online through social media. Movado Group bought it in 2018 for more than $100 million.
history:
Jake Kassan and Kramer LaPlante started MVMT in Los Angeles in June 2013 with the idea of selling stylish, minimalist watches for about $100, far below designer brands. Two Indiegogo campaigns raised more than $290,000, and the pair built the business almost entirely online, using Instagram influencers and Facebook advertising to reach young buyers.

The approach worked: MVMT passed 600,000 watches sold by the end of 2016, expanded into sunglasses and jewelry, and described itself as 'a watch brand by and for millennials'. In 2017 most of its customers were under 34.

In August 2018 Movado Group bought MVMT for more than $100 million, with further payments tied to performance, and the founders later left. Under Movado the brand has broadened its range to include chronographs, solar and automatic divers such as the Cali Diver GMT, while keeping its direct-to-consumer model from its Los Angeles base. MVMT's early watches, like the Classic and the Chrono, had clean dials and quartz movements, and the brand's success inspired a wave of similar online-first watch start-ups. Its marketing relied heavily on travel and lifestyle imagery rather than watchmaking heritage.

name: Naoya Hida & Co.
tagline: Ultra-classical Japanese watches with hand-engraved dials made in tiny numbers
summary: Naoya Hida & Co. is a Tokyo independent making ultra-classical, Calatrava-inspired watches with hand-engraved German silver dials. Produced in runs of a handful to a few dozen pieces, they have become some of the most sought-after Japanese independent watches.
history:
Naoya Hida founded his company in Tokyo in 2018. Before that he had worked on the retail side of high-end watchmaking, representing brands including F.P. Journe, and he set out to make the purely classical watch he felt was missing: small steel cases, time-only or simple complications, and dials engraved by hand rather than printed.

In 2020 master watchmaker Kousuke Fujita, a Hiko Mizuno and WOSTEP graduate who had worked at Seiko and F.P. Journe, joined to handle movement work and assembly. The watches use heavily reworked Swiss movements, for example Valjoux 7750-family calibres stripped of their automatic and chronograph works and converted to manual winding, housed in 904L steel or gold cases. Dials are German silver with hand-engraved numerals filled with urushi lacquer, paired with heat-blued or solid gold hands.

The collection is organised by 'Type': the Type 1 series with small seconds, Type 2 with central seconds, Type 3 moon phases, the rectangular Type 5 of 2024, a perpetual calendar Type 6A in 2025 and, in 2026, its first chronograph using a vintage Valjoux 23-family movement. Each reference is made in very small numbers, usually 2 to 25 pieces, and allocations are heavily oversubscribed.

name: Nezumi Studios
tagline: Stockholm-designed racing chronographs and tool watches, assembled in Germany
summary: Nezumi Studios is a Stockholm design studio founded in 2011 by David Campo that launched its first watch, the Voiture racing chronograph, in 2015. Its affordable, Scandinavian-clean chronographs, divers, GMTs and field watches are designed in Sweden and assembled in Germany.
history:
Nezumi Studios was founded in Stockholm in 2011 by David Campo, a designer and vintage sports-car and watch enthusiast who had spent nearly two decades in the fashion industry and wanted a place with total creative freedom. The studio's first project was not a watch at all but a limited run of 50 pairs of selvedge denim jeans made in Sweden, followed by leather goods and accessories. The name comes from Nezumi Kozō, a Japanese folk hero said to have stolen from rich samurai and given to the poor, reflecting the studio's support for charitable causes.

In 2015 Nezumi launched its first watch, the Voiture, a racing chronograph inspired by 1960s and 1970s motorsport, with a sandwich dial, three sub-registers and a tachymeter bezel. Powered by Seiko's VK mecha-quartz chronograph movement, it offered vintage racing style at an accessible price and quickly became the brand's signature. The Corbeau, a mil-spec-inspired chronograph with a 120-click bezel, and the Tonnerre, with a telemeter scale for measuring distance by the delay between lightning and thunder, extended the chronograph family.

Nezumi later broadened into automatic watches with the Baleine diver, the Aviera GMT with a Miyota 9075 true GMT movement and the Terrain field watch, alongside its own rubber, canvas and leather straps and Colin bracelets. The Voiture VM2 brought a slim automatic column-wheel chronograph to the line. Watches are designed and engineered in Stockholm and assembled, tested and quality-controlled in Germany, and Nezumi remains an independent, founder-led studio.

name: Nicholas Hacko
tagline: Sydney's watchmaker who answered Swiss parts restrictions by building his own movements
summary: Nicholas Hacko is a Sydney master watchmaker, in business since 1981, who with his son Josh turned a repair workshop into Australia's only watch manufacture. After Swiss brands cut off spare parts, he launched the Rebelde brand, then in-house NH-series watches with movements designed and made in Australia, alongside the Soprod-powered Mark 1 and Mark II.
history:
Nicholas Hacko has worked as a master watchmaker, clockmaker and jeweller in Sydney since 1981, running a workshop in the Culwulla Chambers on Castlereagh Street that serviced prestige Swiss watches. Around 2011, as major Swiss brands began restricting the supply of spare parts to independent repairers, his livelihood came under threat. Rather than accept it, Hacko decided to make watches himself, beginning with a defiant '0/9' watch and, in 2013, the Rebelde brand, a 44mm California-dial watch in Pilot's and Control Tower styles, of which more than 700 were sold over six years.

In 2016 Nick and his son Josh, who had been sent to Switzerland for training, decided to build an in-house manufacturing facility in Sydney. They invested in a Citizen CNC lathe for bar-turning screws, pins and pinions, a Kern Pyramid Nano five-axis mill for plates, bridges and dials, an Affolter gear-hobbing machine and a Makino wire EDM. The result was the NH1, a 25-piece titanium watch with a manual-wind calibre manufactured in Australia and described as the first and only watch made there. The NH2 of 2019 became the first watch to use Timascus, a patterned layered-titanium material, in its movement, and the NH3 of 2021 added an in-house titanium guilloché dial and hands.

By 2020 the company could make up to 85 per cent of its watches in-house. Alongside the NH series it produces more accessible models: the Mark 1, a 40mm 1930s-style pilot's watch with a Swiss Soprod M100 movement assembled in Sydney, and the 2023 Mark II, whose anodised titanium dial is guilloché-engraved with waves inspired by Sydney's Curl Curl beach. Total output is around 50 to 100 watches a year.

name: Nivada Grenchen
tagline: Revived 1926 Swiss brand behind the Antarctic, Depthmaster and Chronomaster
summary: Nivada Grenchen is a Swiss brand founded in Grenchen in 1926 and revived in 2018 by Guillaume Laidet. Its faithful reissues of mid-century tool watches such as the Chronomaster Aviator Sea Diver, Antarctic and F77 have made it one of the most successful heritage revivals of recent years.
history:
Nivada was founded in 1926 in Grenchen, in the canton of Solothurn, by Otto Wüllimann, Hermann Schindler and Jakob Schneider, and was registered as Nivada AG in 1932. Through the 1950s and 1960s it became a significant exporter, particularly to the United States where it was distributed through Croton. The brand built a reputation for robust, affordable tool watches: the Antarctic of 1950, linked to expeditions to the polar regions; the Chronomaster Aviator Sea Diver chronograph with its distinctive broad-arrow hands and multi-scale bezel; and the 1964 Depthmaster, rated to 1,000 metres at a time when that was exceptional.

Like many mid-sized Swiss firms, Nivada was badly hurt by the quartz crisis of the 1970s and 1980s, and the name faded into the vintage market, where its chronographs and divers became sought-after collectibles.

In 2018 French entrepreneur Guillaume Laidet, who had previously built the William L. 1985 brand, secured the rights to the name through supplier Rémi Chabrat of the Montrichard Group. Rather than raising capital, Laidet funded production through pre-orders. The relaunch began with the Chronomaster, followed by the Depthmaster, Antarctic, Datomaster, Super Antarctic and the integrated-bracelet F77, which became the brand's best seller. Production reached around 6,000 watches in 2023, and Laidet applied the same revival model to Vulcain and Excelsior Park. Nivada Grenchen marks its centenary in 2026.

name: Nixon
tagline: Surf-and-skate watch brand from Southern California
summary: Nixon was founded in 1997 in Encinitas, California, by Andy Laats and Chad DiNenna to make watches and accessories for the surf, skate and snow crowd. Now based in Carlsbad and co-owned by its founders, Billabong and Trilantic Capital, it is known for models such as the Time Teller and 51-30.
history:
Andy Laats and Chad DiNenna founded Nixon in Encinitas, California, in 1997, aiming to make 'custom built' watches for the action-sports community rather than repurposed fashion pieces. Early models such as the Time Teller and chunky dive and chronograph watches spread through surf and skate shops and team riders.

The brand grew fast, adding bags, headphones and apparel, and in 2006 Australian surf group Billabong bought it for about $55 million plus later payments. In 2012 the founders took control again in a joint venture with Trilantic Capital Partners, returning Nixon to independence; it is now co-owned by Billabong, Trilantic, Laats and DiNenna.

Nixon became known for big, colourful watches such as the 51-30 chronograph, the Sentry, the tide-reading Base and the Regulus digital, and for pop-culture collaborations with Star Wars, Metallica and others. It sells in more than 90 countries and now works mainly through retail partners and its own online store, from headquarters in Carlsbad, California. The brand's name and early marketing leaned on its outsider identity, and its watches were designed to be tough enough for surfing, skating and snowboarding while standing out in bold colours and oversized cases. Nixon's catalogue also covers tide watches for surfers and simple digital models, and it has used limited collaborations to reach music and film fans.

name: Nodus
tagline: Los Angeles microbrand obsessed with engineering details
summary: Nodus Watches was founded in Los Angeles in 2017 by Cullen Chen and Wes Kasper. It designs and assembles tool watches in LA, such as the Sector, Contrail and Unity, and is known for engineering touches like its own crown and bezel systems and the Intersect watch fair.
history:
Cullen Chen and Wes Kasper, two young Los Angeles watch enthusiasts, started Nodus in 2017 with the Trieste dive watch. From the start they did final assembly, regulation and testing in their own Los Angeles workshop, and they described the company as a watch research and design studio rather than just a brand.

Nodus built a reputation for engineering details at affordable prices, including its own crown tubes, bezel click mechanisms and crystal shapes. Models such as the Contrail, a slim travel watch with a Miyota 9075 GMT movement, and the Sector, a family of field, sport and GMT watches with a fast-set jumping GMT hand, sold out in batches.

In 2021 Nodus founded Intersect, a watch-industry gathering that became a joint venture with Formex and Jack Mason, and it runs a Design Lab platform for collaborative designs. Recent releases include the Sector II series with stone dials, full titanium bracelets, the Obscura II and the 36.5 mm Unity with vitreous dials. The founders have kept prices accessible while focusing on robust construction, and most releases are made in limited batches that sell directly to customers.

name: Nomos Glashütte
tagline: Bauhaus-minimal watches with in-house movements at accessible prices
summary: Nomos Glashütte is an independent manufacture founded in 1990, just weeks after the Berlin Wall fell. Its clean, Bauhaus-influenced designs such as the Tangente, combined with in-house calibres and its own Swing System escapement, have made it one of the best-value German watchmakers.
history:
Nomos was founded in Glashütte on 1 January 1990 by Roland Schwertner, a Düsseldorf photographer and IT entrepreneur, taking its name from an earlier Glashütte firm that had briefly traded as Nomos in the early 20th century. The first four models, including the Tangente, appeared in 1992; their slim cases and restrained dials drew on 1930s German design and the functionalist ideals of the Deutscher Werkbund and Bauhaus.

Early Nomos watches used modified Peseux/ETA manual-wind movements, but the company steadily increased its manufacturing depth. It introduced its first self-winding in-house calibre in 2005 and, in 2014, unveiled the Nomos Swing System, its own escapement assembly including balance, hairspring and lever. This made Nomos one of very few independent brands able to produce its own regulating organ.

The ultra-thin DUW 3001 automatic calibre followed in 2015, powering the neomatik line. Nomos remains privately owned and headquartered in Glashütte, with a design studio in Berlin, and it has expanded its range with colourful Club, Tetra and Metro variants, world-timers and limited editions supporting charities such as Doctors Without Borders.

Known for honest pricing and thoughtful design, Nomos is frequently recommended as the entry point into Glashütte watchmaking and has won numerous design awards, including multiple iF and Red Dot prizes.

name: Norqain
tagline: Young, family-owned Swiss sports brand with Kenissi manufacture movements
summary: Norqain is an independent, family-owned Swiss brand founded in 2018 by Ben Küffer and based in Nidau near Biel. It makes adventure-themed sports watches, including the Adventure, Freedom 60, Independence and the ultralight Wild ONE, many powered by manufacture calibres made with Kenissi.
history:
Norqain was founded in 2018 by Ben Küffer, who grew up in a watch-industry family. Founding partners included former NHL player Mark Streit and Ted Schneider, whose family had long owned Breitling.

Norqain launched with the Adventure line, sturdy sports watches in steel and bronze with a distinctive textured 'Norqain plate' personalisation on the side of the case, and the Freedom 60, a vintage-inspired chronograph. A key strategic step came when the brand secured manufacture calibres from Kenissi, the movement maker associated with Tudor, powering models such as the Independence and Adventure Neverest with chronometer-certified automatics and 70-hour power reserves.

In 2022 Norqain introduced the Wild ONE, with a case made of NORTEQ, a lightweight carbon composite, and an integrated shock-absorbing rubber structure, designed to be extremely light and robust. Skeletonised versions and a Wild ONE Skeleton Chrono followed. The brand has built partnerships in ice hockey, including with the NHL, and with Swiss national sports teams and adventure ambassadors. Still independent and family-owned, Norqain has grown rapidly into one of Switzerland's most successful new watch brands. Its growth has been built on a direct relationship with retailers and a deliberately broad line-up spanning steel, bronze, gold and composite cases.

name: Oak & Oscar
tagline: Chicago microbrand making Swiss-powered field, GMT and chronograph watches
summary: Oak & Oscar is an independent Chicago watch company founded in 2015 by Chase Fancher and named after his dog Oscar. Its well-finished Swiss-powered watches, named after figures and places linked to Chicago and the outdoors, have made it one of the most respected American microbrands.
history:
Chase Fancher, a Chicago watch enthusiast, launched Oak & Oscar in 2015. The first watch, the Burnham, was a Swiss automatic field watch named after Daniel Burnham, the architect and planner behind much of Chicago's layout, and it established the brand's style: sandwich dials, orange accents and details such as canvas-and-leather watch wallets.

The brand followed with limited runs such as the Sandford diver and the Jackson flyback chronograph, which sold out quickly, and built a loyal owner community with events and Chicago-themed limited editions, including collaborations with Few Spirits and the US Secret Service.

The core range now consists of the 38 mm Olmsted field watch, named after landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted, the Humboldt GMT with a ceramic 24-hour bezel and anti-magnetic Faraday cage, and the Atwood, a manually wound column-wheel flyback chronograph using a Sellita AMT movement. An 'Experimental Series' has explored in-house finishing and heat-treated components made at the company's Chicago headquarters. The company assembles and tests its watches in small batches and has become known for strong customer relationships, including owners' weekends and events for its community of collectors.

name: Olivia Burton
tagline: Vintage-inspired London watches with bees, florals and British charm
summary: Olivia Burton is a London fashion watch and jewellery brand launched in 2012, known for vintage-inspired women's watches with signature bee motifs, floral dials and mesh bracelets. One of the UK's fastest-growing fashion watch brands, it has been owned by Movado Group since 2017.
history:
Olivia Burton was founded in London and launched in 2012 by Jemma Finch and Lesa Bennett, who set out to create vintage-inspired, design-led watches for women at accessible prices. Drawing on vintage finds, contemporary fashion and a strong sense of British style, the brand quickly became known for small-to-mid-sized dials, floral prints, mesh bracelets and playful details, sold through UK department stores and its own webshop.

Its signature motif became the bee, used on dials, crowns and later jewellery, alongside Mini Dial watches, bee-motif dials and the honeycomb pattern. Collections are often named after London places, such as the Grosvenor, inspired by the clean lines and geometry of London's streets and squares, as well as Westbourne, Highbury and Pembroke. The brand's growth was rapid, and it was widely described as one of the United Kingdom's fastest-growing fashion watch and jewellery brands.

In July 2017 US-based Movado Group, owner of Movado, Concord and Ebel and licensee of brands such as Tommy Hilfiger and Hugo Boss, completed its acquisition of Olivia Burton. Under Movado, the brand expanded internationally and grew its jewellery business, with motifs such as the honeycomb and North Star. Today Olivia Burton's range spans tiny 16mm Mini Grove watches to 30mm Classic Bee and Westbourne designs, mostly with quartz movements and gold, rose-gold, silver and two-tone ion-plated steel cases, with watches designed to be gifted, stacked with bracelets and worn every day.

name: Omega
tagline: The Moonwatch maker and official timekeeper of the Olympic Games
summary: Omega is the Swatch Group's flagship luxury brand, famous for the Speedmaster that went to the Moon, the Seamaster worn by James Bond and its long role as Olympic timekeeper. It pioneered the co-axial escapement and METAS Master Chronometer certification.
history:
Omega began in 1848 when 23-year-old Louis Brandt set up a watch assembly workshop in La Chaux-de-Fonds, buying parts from local craftsmen and selling finished watches across Europe. His sons Louis-Paul and César moved the business to Biel/Bienne in 1880 and adopted industrial, in-house production. Their 19-ligne 'Omega' calibre of 1894, with interchangeable parts, was so successful that the company took the name Louis Brandt & Frère – Omega Watch Co. in 1903.

Omega merged with Tissot in 1930 to form SSIH and in 1932 became official timekeeper of the Los Angeles Olympics, a role it has held at most Games since. Post-war icons followed: the Seamaster (1948), Constellation (1952) and the Speedmaster (1957). NASA qualified the Speedmaster for manned missions in 1965, and on 21 July 1969 Buzz Aldrin wore one on the lunar surface. The following year a Speedmaster helped time the critical engine burn that brought Apollo 13 home.

The quartz crisis hit SSIH hard. In 1983 it merged with ASUAG to create SMH, reorganised by Nicolas Hayek and renamed the Swatch Group in 1998. Under the group Omega was repositioned upmarket, supported by product placement in the James Bond films from GoldenEye (1995) onwards.

In 1999 Omega industrialised George Daniels' co-axial escapement, and in 2015 it launched Master Chronometer certification with the Swiss federal metrology institute METAS, testing complete watches to 15,000 gauss of magnetism. Today, headquartered in Biel, Omega is widely estimated to be the second-largest Swiss luxury watch brand by sales after Rolex.

name: Orient
tagline: In-house Japanese automatics at prices few can match
summary: Orient is a Japanese watchmaker, now part of Seiko Epson, famous for affordable mechanical watches with in-house movements. The Bambino dress watch and the Mako and Kamasu divers are some of the most recommended entry-level automatics in the world.
history:
Orient's roots go back to 1901, when Shogoro Yoshida opened the Yoshida Watch Shop in Tokyo's Ueno district, selling imported pocket watches. The business began manufacturing, and after the Second World War the factory in Hino, Tokyo was reorganized in 1950 as Tama Keiki Co. In 1951 it was renamed Orient Watch Co., and the same year it launched the Orient Star.

Through the 1950s to 70s Orient built a range of mechanical watches for the domestic and export markets, including the Royal Orient and the Orient King Diver. Unlike most Japanese makers, Orient stayed loyal to mechanical watches through the quartz era, which later became its main selling point abroad.

Orient had long cooperated with Seiko Epson, which became its majority owner and made it a subsidiary in 2009. In 2017 Orient Watch Co. was fully merged into Epson, and the brand is now run as Epson's watch business, with movements made at Epson's facilities in Akita and Nagano.

Today Orient is best known in export markets for its value-driven automatics: the domed-crystal Bambino, the Mako diver launched about two decades ago, and the sapphire-equipped Kamasu of 2019, all powered by in-house calibres.

name: Orient Star
tagline: Orient's high-grade 'Shining Star', famous for open-heart and power-reserve dials
summary: Orient Star is the premium line of Orient, created in 1951 to be the 'shining star' of mechanical watches. Now under Seiko Epson, it is known for semi-skeleton dials, power reserve indicators and the M42 Diver 1964 series.
history:
Orient Star was launched in 1951, the same year Tama Keiki was renamed Orient Watch Co. Its name expressed the ambition to create a watch that shines brightest among mechanical timepieces, and the first model was chronometer-grade. Through the 1950s and 60s the line represented Orient's best work, and in 1964 Orient made its first diver's watch, the design source for today's M42 Diver 1964 series.

When quartz swept Japan, Orient continued to invest in mechanical watches. In 1996 it released the first Orient Star with a power reserve indicator, which became the line's signature, followed by world time, GMT and, from the 2000s, the Semi Skeleton and Skeleton models that open up the dial to show the balance wheel.

Orient became a subsidiary of Seiko Epson in 2009 and merged fully into Epson in 2017. Since then Orient Star has been repositioned as a distinct brand with collections such as Classic, Contemporary, Sports and M-Line, using Epson's precision finishing and the F6 and F8 calibres.

In the current range, the Classic Semi Skeleton pairs an open window over the balance with the signature power reserve indicator, while the M42 Diver 1964 2nd Edition offers a 41 mm, 200 m diver with sapphire crystal and the F6N47 calibre. Orient Star is positioned as the more refined, better-finished sibling of the value-focused Orient line.

name: Oris
tagline: Independent Swiss mechanical watches, 'Go your own way' since 1904
summary: Oris is one of the few independent Swiss watch companies, making only mechanical watches, recognisable by the red rotor. Its Aquis and Divers Sixty-Five divers, Big Crown pilot's watches and in-house Calibre 400 offer strong value in the Swiss mid-range.
history:
Oris was founded in 1904 by Paul Cattin and Georges Christian, who bought a disused watch factory in the village of Hölstein near Basel and named their company after a nearby brook. The business grew rapidly, becoming the largest employer in the area and building housing for workers; by the late 1920s it ran several factories. Swiss cartel rules limited Oris to pin-lever escapements until the 1960s, but it still produced hundreds of calibres.

In 1938 Oris launched the Big Crown, a pilot's watch whose oversized crown could be operated with gloves and whose pointer-date hand became a signature. The Divers Sixty-Five of 1965 and early alarm and chronograph models followed. Oris joined the ASUAG conglomerate in 1970, and during the quartz crisis its workforce shrank dramatically.

In 1982 managers Dr Rolf Portmann and Ulrich W. Herzog led a buyout, making Oris independent again. They decided to make only mechanical watches, an unusual bet at the height of the quartz era, adopted the red rotor as a signature and repositioned the brand around four worlds: diving, aviation, motor sport and culture. The Aquis dive watch arrived in 2011 and the Divers Sixty-Five reissue in 2015.

Oris returned to in-house movement making with the hand-wound, ten-day Calibre 110 in 2014 for its 110th anniversary, and in 2020 introduced Calibre 400, an automatic with a five-day power reserve, high anti-magnetism and a ten-year warranty. It has become known for environmental and social projects, such as dials made from upcycled plastic. Oris remains headquartered in Hölstein and privately owned.

name: Otsuka Lotec
tagline: Industrial-machine aesthetics and jumping hours from a one-man Tokyo workshop
summary: Otsuka Lotec is the brand of Tokyo designer-watchmaker Jiro Katayama, who makes watches that look like pieces of vintage industrial equipment. His jumping-hour and retrograde displays, turret windows and meter-like dials have made the brand a cult favourite among independent collectors.
history:
Jiro Katayama, a product designer by training, began making watches around 2008 after buying a used bench lathe in an online auction. Working from a small workshop in Tokyo, he taught himself to machine cases and modules, drawing inspiration from the forms, textures and details of old industrial objects such as gauges, meters and machinery.

Otsuka Lotec began selling watches commercially in 2012. Its numbered models, such as No. 5, No. 6 and No. 7, combine Japanese Miyota base movements with Katayama's own complication modules: the No. 6 shows retrograde hours and minutes on a fan-shaped meter, while the No. 7 and No. 7.5 display a jumping hour through turret-shaped windows with rotating minute and second discs. Demand quickly outstripped his tiny output, and pieces became famous for being nearly impossible to buy.

In 2023 the core models were redesigned with upgraded materials. The brand has since expanded upward with the No. 9, a rectangular piece with an in-house manual movement combining jumping hours, rewinding minutes, a tourbillon and hour striking, and the No. 8 of 2026. Otsuka Lotec watches are displayed permanently at Isetan Shinjuku.

name: Pagani Design
tagline: Guangzhou's sapphire-crystal homage watches at bargain prices
summary: Pagani Design is a Chinese watch brand founded in Guangzhou in 2012 by Guangzhou Pagani Design Watch Co., Ltd. It is best known for inexpensive homage-style watches, echoing famous Swiss designs, with 316L steel cases, sapphire crystals and Japanese or Chinese movements, sold worldwide largely online.
history:
Pagani Design was established in Guangzhou, southern China, in 2012. Guangzhou and the surrounding Pearl River Delta are the heart of China's watch-making supply chain, and the brand grew out of that ecosystem with a straightforward proposition: make the look and specification of higher-end watches accessible to everyone. Its stated philosophy is that true horology should be defined by excellence rather than exclusivity.

The brand became widely known through online marketplaces such as AliExpress and Amazon, where its models, designated by 'PD' reference numbers, gained a following among budget-conscious enthusiasts. Many Pagani Design watches are openly inspired by iconic Swiss designs, including racing chronographs with tachymeter bezels, GMT travellers, fluted-bezel dress-sports watches and dive watches, while offering specifications unusual at their price, such as sapphire crystals, screw-down crowns, ceramic bezels and 100-200m water resistance. Movements include Seiko VK63 meca-quartz and Miyota quartz chronographs, Miyota 8215 automatics and Chinese Pearl GMT calibres.

In recent years the company has worked to strengthen its brand, launching an official global web store with a three-year warranty to distinguish genuine products from grey-market sellers, operating warehouses in the US, UK and Europe, and adding more ambitious pieces such as affordable mechanical tourbillons in its YS series. Pagani Design also operates the sister brand Benyar. It now sells across Europe, the Americas, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and Africa, and is one of the best-known names in the Chinese affordable-watch segment.

name: Panerai
tagline: Florentine naval divers' watches with a cult following
summary: Panerai began as a Florentine supplier of precision instruments to the Italian Navy and now makes its big cushion-cased Luminor and Radiomir watches in Neuchâtel for Richemont. Its crown-protecting bridge and sandwich dials are instantly recognisable.
history:
Giovanni Panerai opened a watch shop and workshop on Florence's Ponte alle Grazie in 1860. His grandson Guido turned the family business towards precision instruments for the Royal Italian Navy, and in 1916 Panerai patented Radiomir, a radium-based luminous paste for gun sights and dials.

In 1936 Panerai built prototype diving watches for the frogmen of the Navy's First Submarine Group Command, using large cushion-shaped cases and movements supplied by Rolex, with Panerai making the luminous dials. The Radiomir went into service in 1938, and wartime experience led to features such as the 'sandwich' dial, with numerals cut through a top plate over a luminous layer. In 1949 Panerai registered Luminor, a tritium-based compound, and in the 1950s patented the lever-operated crown-protecting bridge that defines the Luminor case. The Egiziano, a 60mm giant, was made for the Egyptian Navy in 1956. In total only a few hundred to a few thousand military watches were delivered.

After the military contracts ended, Panerai launched its first civilian collection in 1993. Sylvester Stallone wore a Luminor in the 1996 film Daylight and ordered special editions for friends, spreading the brand in Hollywood. In 1997 the Vendôme group, now Richemont, bought Panerai and turned it into an international luxury brand, relocating production to Switzerland.

Panerai opened a manufacture in Neuchâtel in 2002 and introduced its first in-house calibre, the P.2002, in 2005. Since then it has expanded its in-house movement range and developed materials such as BMG-Tech metallic glass, Carbotech and recycled eSteel. The Luminor, Radiomir, Submersible and Luminor Due collections continue the Italian naval design that attracts devoted collectors known as 'Paneristi'.

name: Parmigiani Fleurier
tagline: A master restorer's manufacture in Fleurier, backed by the Sandoz Family Foundation
summary: Parmigiani Fleurier was founded in 1996 by master restorer Michel Parmigiani with the backing of the Sandoz Family Foundation. Vertically integrated through its sister companies, including movement maker Vaucher, it is known for refined, understated watches such as the Tonda PF with its knurled bezel.
history:
Michel Parmigiani, born in 1950, trained as a watchmaker in Fleurier and in 1976 opened his own workshop, Parmigiani Mesure et Art du Temps, specialising in the restoration of antique clocks, automata and complicated pocket watches. His skill brought him to the attention of the Sandoz Family Foundation, the charitable holding of the pharmaceutical family, for whom he restored its important collection of historic timepieces.

In 1996 the foundation acquired a majority of his business and launched Parmigiani Fleurier as a watch brand, debuting with the Toric collection, whose knurled bezel recalled classical architectural ornament. The Kalpa tonneau followed in 1998. Over the next decade the foundation built a remarkable network of suppliers in the Val-de-Travers: Vaucher Manufacture Fleurier for movements, Les Artisans Boîtiers for cases, Quadrance et Habillage for dials and Atokalpa for components. Vaucher also supplies movements to other brands, and Hermès took a stake in it in 2006.

Parmigiani became known for exceptional finishing, for bespoke pieces and for a long partnership with Bugatti that produced the Bugatti Type 370 in 2004, with its transverse, engine-like movement. It also restored and built unique objects, from pocket watches to clocks.

In 2019 Guido Terreni, previously of Bulgari, became CEO and refocused the brand around quiet luxury. The Tonda PF, launched in 2021 with an integrated bracelet, platinum knurled bezel and barleycorn guilloché dial, became the brand's breakthrough success. The Tonda PF Minute Rattrapante and the relaunched Toric followed, and Parmigiani remains owned by the Sandoz Family Foundation.

name: Patek Philippe
tagline: Geneva's family-owned benchmark for grand complications since 1839
summary: Patek Philippe is widely regarded as the most prestigious watch manufacturer in the world, famed for its grand complications, perpetual calendars and the Nautilus. Owned by the Stern family since 1932, it remains one of the last independent, family-run Genevan manufactures and dominates the high end of the auction market.
history:
Patek Philippe traces its origins to 1839, when Polish émigrés Antoni Patek and Franciszek Czapek founded Patek, Czapek & Co. in Geneva. After the partners split in 1844, Patek teamed up with French watchmaker Jean Adrien Philippe, inventor of a keyless winding and hand-setting system, and in 1851 the firm became Patek Philippe & Co. Royal clients followed quickly: Queen Victoria acquired a Patek pendant watch at the 1851 Great Exhibition in London.

The firm built its reputation on precision and complications. It made what is considered the first Swiss wristwatch in 1868 for the Hungarian Countess Koscowicz, the first perpetual-calendar wristwatch in 1925, and in 1933 delivered the Henry Graves Jr. Supercomplication, a pocket watch with 24 complications that sold for more than CHF 23 million in 2014.

The Great Depression brought the company to the brink, and in 1932 it was bought by Charles and Jean Stern, owners of a dial-making firm. The Stern family has controlled it ever since, passing leadership from Henri Stern to Philippe Stern and, in 2009, to Thierry Stern. The brand weathered the quartz crisis by staying resolutely mechanical and, in 1976, launched Gérald Genta's steel Nautilus, which would later become one of the most sought-after watches in the world. The 1989 Calibre 89, with 33 complications, marked the company's 150th anniversary.

In 1996 Patek consolidated production at a large manufacture in Plan-les-Ouates outside Geneva, and in 2009 it replaced the Geneva Seal with its own stricter Patek Philippe Seal. Today it produces an estimated 70,000 watches a year, discontinued the fabled Nautilus 5711 in 2021, launched the Cubitus in 2024, and still consistently holds the record for the most expensive wristwatches ever sold at auction.

name: Perrelet
tagline: Named for the inventor of the self-winding watch, famed for the Turbine
summary: Perrelet honours Abraham-Louis Perrelet, the Le Locle watchmaker credited with inventing the self-winding mechanism around 1777. Revived in 1995 and owned by Spain's Festina Group since 2004, the Biel-based brand is best known for its Double Rotor and spinning-blade Turbine watches.
history:
Abraham-Louis Perrelet (1728–1826) was a watchmaker from Le Locle who, around 1777, developed a self-winding mechanism using an oscillating weight set in motion by the wearer's walking. The Geneva Society of Arts reported that about fifteen minutes of walking would wind the watch for eight days. His invention influenced Abraham-Louis Breguet, who developed his own 'perpétuelle' self-winding watches, and Perrelet is widely credited as the father of the automatic watch.

The modern Perrelet brand was established in 1995 in his honour. Its first signature product, the Double Rotor, placed a visible rotating weight on the dial side synchronised with the conventional rotor on the back, making the automatic winding itself part of the display. In 2004 the brand was acquired by the Spanish Festina Group, which also owns Candino and Jaguar, and it is based in Biel/Bienne.

In 2009 Perrelet introduced the Turbine, whose dial is covered by a set of titanium blades, inspired by jet engines, that spin freely with the motion of the wrist to reveal the dial beneath. The Turbine became the brand's bestseller and spawned many variations, from the Turbine Toxic to Turbine Pilot and Diver versions. Perrelet also produced complications priced well into six figures, the Lab Peripheral with its peripheral rotor, and in 2021 the P-331-MH in-house calibre with COSC certification. The brand produces around 30,000 watches a year.

name: Petermann Bédat
tagline: Two young Vaud watchmakers reviving dead-beat seconds and rattrapantes
summary: Petermann Bédat is an independent atelier in Renens near Lausanne founded by Gaël Petermann and Florian Bédat, who met at the Geneva watchmaking school. Its hand-finished Reference 1967 dead-beat seconds and Reference 2941 monopusher split-seconds chronograph are made in editions of just ten.
history:
Gaël Petermann and Florian Bédat met as students at the Geneva watchmaking school and went on to work in Switzerland and Germany, including in restoration and haute horlogerie workshops, before joining forces to create their own atelier in Renens, near Lausanne.

Their first watch, the Reference 1967, arrived in 2018: a dead-beat seconds wristwatch with an in-house calibre, inspired by pocket-watch architecture and German-school finishing, with a semi-open sapphire dial ringed in sandblasted steel. It was made in only ten pieces each in rose and white gold and quickly made them names to watch among collectors.

They followed with the Reference 2941, a platinum monopusher split-seconds chronograph with a jumping minute counter and their Calibre 202, again limited to ten pieces, and more recently the Reference 1825, a purist three-hand watch with a redesigned calibre. The pair continue to hand-finish every component in their small workshop. Their approach favours small, hand-made batches over growth: each watch is assembled, finished and regulated in-house, with traditional techniques such as bevelling, perlage and Côtes de Genève applied by hand. Collectors have embraced them as leading representatives of a new generation of Swiss independents.

name: Philippe Dufour
tagline: The Vallée de Joux master whose Simplicity defined independent watchmaking
summary: Philippe Dufour is a watchmaker from Le Sentier in the Vallée de Joux whose three wristwatches - the Grande Sonnerie, Duality and Simplicity - are regarded as benchmarks of hand-finishing. Made in tiny numbers, they now command seven-figure prices at auction.
history:
Born in 1948 in Le Sentier, Philippe Dufour trained at the Vallée de Joux watchmaking school and worked for Jaeger-LeCoultre, Gérald Genta and Audemars Piguet, including stints abroad teaching and servicing complicated watches. In 1978 he set up his own workshop in Le Sentier, restoring antique pieces and building complicated movements for other houses.

In 1992 he unveiled the first wristwatch with a grande and petite sonnerie with minute repeater, a stunning achievement for a lone artisan, and made only four examples. In 1996 came the Duality, the first wristwatch with two balance wheels linked by a differential, of which only nine were made. His 2000 Simplicity, a time-only watch with small seconds and an obsessively hand-finished movement, was produced in about 200 examples (in 34mm and 37mm) and became the archetypal collector's grail of the independent movement.

Dufour largely stopped serial production in the 2010s, though a 20th-anniversary Simplicity series was delivered in the early 2020s and he continues to make occasional unique pieces for charity. His influence on younger independents - through mentoring and his insistence on traditional hand-finishing - is immense, and his watches regularly sell for well over a million dollars.

name: Piaget
tagline: Ultra-thin movement specialist and master of gold, gems and colour
summary: Piaget grew from a 19th-century movement workshop in the Jura into a Richemont-owned maison famous for ultra-thin watchmaking and jewellery watches. Its Altiplano holds multiple thinness records, while the Piaget Polo is one of the original luxury integrated-bracelet designs.
history:
In 1874 Georges Édouard Piaget set up a workshop in his family farmhouse in La Côte-aux-Fées, in the Swiss Jura, making high-precision movements and components for other brands. For decades the company worked anonymously as a supplier until his grandsons Gérald and Valentin Piaget registered the Piaget name in 1943 and began selling complete watches under their own brand.

The post-war years established the house's two pillars. In 1957 Valentin Piaget developed the calibre 9P, a hand-wound movement just 2 mm thick, and in 1960 the 12P, then the world's thinnest self-winding movement at 2.3 mm, which earned a place in the Guinness Book of Records. The thin movements freed space for creativity, and from 1964 Piaget pioneered hard-stone dials in lapis lazuli, turquoise, onyx and tiger's eye. In 1959 it opened a Geneva workshop for gold-setting and jewellery, and its bold gold cuff watches became emblems of 1960s and 70s glamour worn by Andy Warhol and Hollywood stars.

In 1979 Yves Piaget launched the Piaget Polo, an all-gold watch whose horizontal gadroons flowed seamlessly from case to bracelet, and it became a symbol of 1980s luxury. The family sold the company to the Vendôme group, now Richemont, in 1988, although Yves Piaget remained an ambassador. Manufacturing is split between La Côte-aux-Fées for movements and Plan-les-Ouates near Geneva for cases, jewellery and assembly.

In the 21st century Piaget returned to record-breaking: the Altiplano Ultimate Concept became the world's thinnest mechanical watch at 2 mm in 2018 and entered series production in 2020. The Polo was relaunched as a steel sports watch in 2016 and again in 2021, and the house celebrated its 150th anniversary in 2024 with a re-edition of the Polo 79.

name: Poljot
tagline: The First Moscow Watch Factory brand that timed Gagarin's flight and Leonov's spacewalk
summary: Poljot ('flight') was the brand of the First Moscow Watch Factory, founded in 1930, whose Sturmanskie was worn by Yuri Gagarin and whose Strela chronograph went on the first spacewalk. The Soviet-era factory has since closed; the name lives on through Poljot-International in Alzenau, Germany.
history:
The First State Watch Factory was established in Moscow in 1930, using machinery and tooling bought from the defunct Dueber-Hampden company in the United States, and was later named after Sergei Kirov. It produced the first mass-market Soviet watches and, after the war, pilot's watches such as the Sturmanskie ('navigator's'), a version of which Yuri Gagarin wore on the first human spaceflight in 1961. Following that flight, the factory's watches took the name Poljot, meaning 'flight'.

In 1959 the factory introduced the Strela chronograph with calibre 3017, issued to Soviet pilots and cosmonauts; Alexei Leonov wore one during the first spacewalk in 1965. From the 1970s the factory produced the calibre 3133 chronograph, based on the Swiss Valjoux 7734, which powered the Okeah naval chronograph and many export Poljot chronographs.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union the factory was privatised and struggled, and Poljot-branded movement production eventually ceased. In 1992 the distributor Poljot-V GmbH was founded in Frankfurt, and in 1994 the Poljot-International brand was created under Alexander Shorokhov. Now based in Alzenau, Germany, Poljot-International designs and assembles mechanical watches inspired by the Russian tradition, while the Sturmanskie and Strela names are used separately by other Russian companies.

name: Prim
tagline: Czechoslovakia's national watch, made in Nové Město nad Metují since 1949
summary: Prim is the Czech watch brand born in 1949 when the state enterprise Chronotechna set out to build Czechoslovakia's first wristwatches in Nové Město nad Metují. Millions of 'Primky' were made, and today the brand produces its own manufacture calibres alongside heritage models such as the Spartak and Orlík.
history:
On 6 November 1949, Adolf Martínek and fifteen colleagues set up a new branch of the national enterprise Chronotechna in an empty building in Nové Město nad Metují, tasked with making the first Czechoslovak wristwatches. Using calculations based on the French Lip R25 calibre, they produced twelve prototypes in 1954 under the name Spartak. Serial production began in 1957, and at the end of that year a ministerial commission decided the wristwatches would carry the Prim name, previously used for alarm and wall clocks. The first watches reached customers in 1958.

The 1960s brought the models that defined the brand, including the Pavouk, the Diplomat, the Sport and the Orlík, developed in 1965 for the Czechoslovak army. In 1969 the factory became independent from Chronotechna as Elton, and by the end of the 1980s around 15 million Prim watches had been made in Nové Město.

Privatisation after 1990 split the business: the Frýdek-Místek operation obtained the PRIM trademarks in 2001, starting a dispute over the brand that lasted more than twenty years. In June 2025 Petr Hanko, owner of MPM-Quality, bought Elton hodinářská from the CSG group, reuniting the brand, and in 2026 a unified logo based on the 1956 original was introduced. Prim now makes watches in both Nové Město nad Metují, home to its manufacture calibres, and Frýdek-Místek.

name: Rado
tagline: The master of materials, pioneer of scratch-resistant and ceramic watches
summary: Rado is the Swatch Group's materials specialist, famous for scratch-resistant hardmetal and high-tech ceramic watches. Its DiaStar, Captain Cook and True collections combine modern design with durable, lightweight materials.
history:
Rado grew out of Schlup & Co., a movement factory founded in 1917 in Lengnau, near Biel, by brothers Fritz, Ernst and Werner Schlup. For decades it supplied movements to other brands. After the Second World War the company began producing its own watches, and in 1957 it introduced the Rado name with the Golden Horse collection.

Rado found its identity in materials. In 1962 it launched the DiaStar, widely described as the world's first scratch-resistant watch, with a case in hardmetal (a tungsten-carbide alloy) and a faceted sapphire crystal. The same year it introduced the Captain Cook diver. Rado became part of ASUAG in 1971 and, through the 1983 merger with SSIH, part of the Swatch Group.

In 1986 Rado launched the Integral, the first of its watches to use high-tech ceramic for the bracelet, and in 1990 the Ceramica with an all-ceramic case and bracelet. The 1998 V10K used ultra-hard diamond-like coatings, and in 2011 Rado introduced plasma high-tech ceramic, with a metallic grey appearance but no metal content. Other developments included monobloc ceramic cases, the ultra-light Ceramos composite, and colour ceramics.

Rado's recent success has come from the reissued Captain Cook, relaunched in 2017, and the True Square and True Thinline collections, often designed with outside designers such as Tej Chauhan and Konstantin Grcic. Headquartered in Lengnau, Rado remains one of the Swatch Group's key brands in Asia and the Middle East, known for hard-wearing watches at mid-range prices.

name: Raketa
tagline: Peter the Great's 1721 Peterhof factory, making watches named for Gagarin's flight
summary: Raketa is the watch brand of the Petrodvorets (Peterhof) Watch Factory near St Petersburg, founded as Peter the Great's imperial lapidary works in 1721. Named in honour of Gagarin's 1961 flight, it is one of the few factories that makes every part of its movements, including hairsprings.
history:
Peter the Great founded the Imperial Peterhof Factory in 1721 beside his summer palace outside St Petersburg to cut and carve hardstones for the new imperial capital. For two centuries it produced lavish stone objects as imperial gifts, and in Soviet times it made monumental works such as the Kremlin stars. In 1938 the factory began producing ruby jewels for watch movements.

After the Second World War, the factory launched the Pobeda watch in 1945 on the Kremlin's orders, and in 1961 the Raketa ('rocket') brand was created in honour of Yuri Gagarin's first human spaceflight. Raketa became one of the Soviet Union's largest watchmakers, developing the 24-hour Polar watch for the Soviet Antarctic Expedition in 1970, the famous Big Zero, and the official watches of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

After a difficult period following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the factory began a modernisation programme in 2011 with new investors, reviving Soviet-era designs and investing in its own manufacturing. Raketa now produces every part of its mechanical movements in Peterhof, including the hairspring, and has introduced its own automatic calibre and playful designs such as the Copernicus and the counterclockwise Russian Code. In 2021 the factory celebrated its 300th anniversary.

name: Raymond Weil
tagline: Family-owned Geneva watchmaker inspired by music and the arts
summary: Raymond Weil is an independent, family-run Geneva brand founded in 1976, known for accessible Swiss watches whose collections are named after music and opera. It is now led by the founder's grandson, Elie Bernheim.
history:
Raymond Weil founded his company in Geneva in 1976, in the middle of the quartz crisis, after more than two decades in the watch industry, together with partner Simone Bédat. Betting that there was room for an independent brand, he offered well-made Swiss watches, initially mostly quartz, at accessible prices, and built a distribution network across dozens of countries.

Weil's love of the arts shaped the brand's identity. Early collections included Golden Eagle and Amadeus, and later lines were given musical and operatic names such as Othello, Fidelio, Parsifal, Tango, Toccata and Maestro. The ultra-thin Othello of 1983 and the gold-and-steel Parsifal of 1988 were among its early successes, and the brand became well known for advertising and for partnerships with musicians and music institutions.

The company remained in family hands. Weil's son-in-law Olivier Bernheim became president in 1996, and in 2014, the year Raymond Weil died, his grandson Elie Bernheim became CEO, with his brother Pierre Bernheim also in the business. Under the third generation the brand developed limited editions with music icons such as the Beatles, David Bowie, AC/DC and Gibson guitars.

In 2016 Raymond Weil introduced Calibre RW1212, its first in-house-developed movement made in collaboration with Sellita, featuring an open balance, in the Freelancer sports collection. Recent years have brought the Millesime vintage-inspired line and new integrated-bracelet Freelancers. Raymond Weil remains independent and headquartered in Geneva, one of the few family-owned Swiss brands of its size.

name: Ressence
tagline: Belgian design-led watches that tell time with rotating discs, not hands
summary: Ressence is a Belgian brand founded in Antwerp in 2010 by industrial designer Benoît Mintiens. Its patented ROCS system displays time on orbiting, convex discs, and oil-filled models like the Type 3 make the display look printed on the crystal.
history:
Benoît Mintiens, an industrial designer who had worked on products from trains to consumer goods, founded Ressence in Antwerp in 2010. The name blends 'renaissance' and 'essence'. The ZeroSeries (Type 1001) debuted at Baselworld 2010, introducing a dial with no conventional hands: instead, a set of discs and sub-discs rotate in orbit around one another, driven by a module mounted on a modified Swiss automatic base.

The system, later called ROCS (Ressence Orbital Convex System), evolved through the Type 1 and, in 2013, the Type 3, whose upper chamber is filled with oil. The fluid eliminates internal reflection so the dial seems to sit on the surface of the crystal; the Type 3 won the Horological Revelation prize at the 2013 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève. The oil-filled Type 5 diver (2015) stayed legible underwater at any angle, and the cushion-cased Type 1 Squared followed in 2017. Early models had no crown at all, being set and wound through a rotating caseback lever.

Later innovations included the Type 2 with its e-Crown electromechanical setting system, the minimalist Type 8, and collaborations such as a Type 3 with designer Marc Newson. The company, headquartered in Antwerp, remains an independent, design-led outlier in a Swiss-dominated field.

name: RGM
tagline: Pennsylvania's master watchmaker, building American movements by hand
summary: RGM Watch Co. was founded in 1992 by watchmaker Roland G. Murphy in Mount Joy, Pennsylvania. It is one of the only American companies to design and make its own movements, including the Caliber 801, the Caliber 20 and the Pennsylvania Tourbillon, and it does hand engine-turning and enamel work in-house.
history:
Roland G. Murphy studied watchmaking at the Bowman Technical School in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and at the WOSTEP school in Switzerland, then worked for Hamilton before founding RGM in 1992. Early RGM watches used Swiss movements in cases and dials designed in Pennsylvania, and the brand became known for special pieces for railway enthusiasts and military units, such as the Corps of Engineers watches.

Murphy's larger ambition was to revive American movement-making. In 2007 RGM completed the Caliber 801, a manual-wind movement produced in-house, making it the first American company in decades to make its own mechanical movement in series. It was followed by the Pennsylvania Tourbillon and, for the brand's 20th anniversary, the Caliber 20, whose motor barrel and moonphase recall the best American railroad pocket watches.

RGM also invested in rose-engine and straight-line engine-turning machines to make guilloché dials by hand, and offers Grand Feu enamel dials. Still a small, independent family workshop in Mount Joy, the company also restores vintage watches and makes pieces to order, from the Swiss-powered Model 151 pilot's watch to high-end Caliber 801 pieces.

name: Richard Mille
tagline: Racing machines on the wrist: ultra-light tonneau hyper-watches since 2001
summary: Richard Mille launched in 2001 and in two decades became one of the most valuable watch brands in the world, with an estimated CHF 1.75 billion in revenue from only about 6,000 watches a year. Its technical, tonneau-shaped watches in carbon TPT, titanium and ceramic are worn by elite athletes such as Rafael Nadal.
history:
Richard Mille, a French executive who had worked in watch and jewellery marketing at Matra and Mauboussin, set out in the late 1990s to build a watch using the materials and engineering logic of Formula 1 and aerospace. He partnered with Dominique Guenat, whose family business Horométrie in Les Breuleux in the Jura would manufacture the watches, and with the movement specialist Audemars Piguet Renaud & Papi. The first model, the RM 001 tourbillon, was presented in 2001 at a price that astonished the industry.

The brand's principle was that watches should be as comfortable and resistant as sports equipment. Its tonneau cases, skeletonised movements with titanium baseplates and innovative materials such as Carbon TPT and Quartz TPT made a distinctive visual language. Racing driver Felipe Massa wore the RM 011 flyback chronograph, launched in 2007, and in 2010 Rafael Nadal began competing with the RM 027 tourbillon, which weighed under 20 grams. Nadal won major titles wearing the watches, turning the brand into a global phenomenon.

Richard Mille remains independent and family controlled, with the Mille and Guenat families holding the business, and the founder's children now in senior roles. Production is deliberately limited to around 6,000 pieces a year, yet according to Morgan Stanley estimates the brand ranked sixth in the Swiss industry in 2025. Recent records include the RM UP-01 Ferrari of 2022, at 1.75 mm the thinnest mechanical watch at its launch, and the RM 27-05 for Nadal. Ambassadors range from Formula 1 driver Charles Leclerc to sprinters and golfers, and a women's collection has grown around the RM 07-01.

name: Roger Dubuis
tagline: Geneva hyper-watches: skeletonised star bridges and Lamborghini links
summary: Roger Dubuis is a Geneva-based Richemont maison founded in 1995, known for flamboyant skeletonised watches with star-shaped bridges and long-standing adherence to the Geneva Seal. Its Excalibur and Knights of the Round Table collections, plus a partnership with Lamborghini Squadra Corse, define its 'hyper horology' positioning.
history:
Roger Dubuis was founded in Geneva in 1995 by watchmaker Roger Dubuis, who had spent years in the complications workshop of Patek Philippe, and the entrepreneur Carlos Dias. Its first collections, Hommage and Sympathie, were classical in design, but the company quickly distinguished itself by committing to have its movements certified with the Geneva Seal, the Poinçon de Genève, and by building its own manufacture in Meyrin.

In the 2000s the brand developed a bolder identity. The Excalibur, with its fluted bezel and triple lugs, became the flagship, and the Easy Diver and Golden Square added sportier and more exuberant shapes. The company produced large numbers of in-house calibres, including tourbillons and skeleton movements, in a remarkably short time.

Richemont took a 60% stake in 2008 and later full control, and after the founder stepped back the brand pivoted to what it calls 'hyper horology'. The star-shaped skeleton bridge became its signature, most notably in the Excalibur Double Flying Tourbillon and the Spider series. The Knights of the Round Table collection turned Arthurian figures into miniature sculptures around the dial. In 2017 Roger Dubuis partnered with Lamborghini Squadra Corse and Pirelli, launching Excalibur models with motorsport materials, rubber straps made from tyre compounds and the high-energy Monovortex and Duotor mechanisms.

Roger Dubuis himself died in 2017. Under Richemont the brand continues to produce limited, highly technical watches, typically in carbon, titanium, ceramic and composite cases, positioned firmly at the top end of the market.

name: Roger W. Smith
tagline: George Daniels' only apprentice, hand-making watches on the Isle of Man
summary: Roger W. Smith OBE is widely regarded as the world's finest living watchmaker, the protégé of George Daniels. His small Isle of Man workshop makes around 15–20 watches a year entirely by hand using the Daniels Method, each built around a co-axial escapement.
history:
Roger Smith enrolled at the Manchester School of Horology at 16 in 1986, winning the British Horological Institute's Bronze Medal as its top student. After hearing George Daniels lecture, he resolved to make a watch entirely by hand, and completed his first pocket watch, with a one-minute tourbillon and detent escapement, at 22. Daniels rejected it as not good enough; Smith's second pocket watch, adding a perpetual calendar, won Daniels' approval.

Daniels then invited Smith to the Isle of Man to help create the Daniels Millennium series of co-axial wristwatches, making him Daniels' only apprentice. Smith subsequently founded Roger W. Smith Ltd in a converted bedroom in Ballaugh, Isle of Man, beginning with a series of unique tourbillon wristwatches.

In 2004 he began designing the Series 2, finishing the prototype in 2006; it was the first production movement designed specifically around the Daniels co-axial escapement. Over the following years he refined the co-axial into his own single-wheel version. Later came the Series 1, 3, 4 (whose first piece, delivered in 2020, was the 100th watch made under his name), 5 and 6.

Smith was awarded an OBE in 2018 for services to British watchmaking and continues to lead a small team making almost every component in-house, producing around 15 to 20 watches a year with waiting lists of several years.

name: Rolex
tagline: The crown of Swiss watchmaking and the world's most recognised luxury watch
summary: Rolex is the largest and most valuable luxury watch brand in the world, known for robust, vertically integrated Oyster watches such as the Submariner, Daytona and Datejust. Owned by a charitable foundation, it combines conservative evolutionary design with in-house everything, from gold alloys to hairsprings.
history:
Rolex began in London in 1905, when Bavarian-born Hans Wilsdorf and his brother-in-law Alfred Davis founded Wilsdorf & Davis to import Swiss movements and case them as wristwatches, then still seen as a fad. Wilsdorf registered the Rolex name in 1908, and in 1910 a Rolex became the first wristwatch to receive an official Swiss chronometer certificate. High wartime taxes pushed the company to Geneva in 1919.

The 1920s and 1930s defined the brand. The hermetically sealed Oyster case of 1926 was publicised when Mercedes Gleitze wore one while swimming the English Channel in 1927, and the Perpetual self-winding rotor followed in 1931. After the war came the Datejust (1945), the Submariner and Explorer (1953), the GMT-Master (1955), the Day-Date (1956) and the Cosmograph Daytona (1963), a family of professional and classic models that still forms the core catalogue.

When Wilsdorf's wife died in 1944 he created the Hans Wilsdorf Foundation, and on his death in 1960 it became the sole owner of Rolex, which remains private and does not publish figures. Rolex weathered the quartz crisis by staying with mechanical watches, briefly offering the quartz Oysterquartz, and by positioning itself as a status symbol rather than a mere instrument.

Since the 2000s Rolex has integrated its supply chain almost completely, casting its own gold and platinum alloys, making Parachrom hairsprings and Cerachrom ceramic bezels, and introducing a new generation of calibres with the Chronergy escapement. Its 2023 purchase of the retailer Bucherer and the Rolex Certified Pre-Owned programme show a move into distribution. Industry estimates put annual output above one million watches and sales above CHF 10 billion, several times its nearest rival, and demand for its steel sports models has outstripped supply for years.

name: Romain Gauthier
tagline: Vallée de Joux precision engineer turned maker of constant-force masterpieces
summary: Romain Gauthier is a Le Sentier manufacture founded by a Vallée de Joux-born precision engineer. Its Logical One, with a chain-and-snail-cam constant-force system, and the hand-finished Insight Micro-Rotor and C by Romain Gauthier have made it a respected technical independent, with Chanel as a minority shareholder.
history:
Born in the Vallée de Joux in 1975, Romain Gauthier trained in precision mechanics and worked in the region's component industry, including programming CNC machines for high-end movement parts, before studying business. In 2002 he set up his own company in Le Sentier, initially making components for other brands, while developing his own watches.

His first watch, the Prestige HM with an in-house movement, arrived in the mid-2000s and was followed by the Prestige HMS in 2012. In 2013 he launched the Logical One, which re-imagined the fusée-and-chain constant-force system with a compact snail-shaped cam and a ruby-link chain, earning GPHG recognition and becoming the brand's signature.

Chanel acquired a minority stake in the company, one of its first moves into independent watchmaking, while Gauthier kept control. Later models included the Insight Micro-Rotor, with an off-centre dial and extensive hand finishing, and in 2021 C by Romain Gauthier, a sportier titanium watch with an integrated bracelet. The manufacture, still based in Le Sentier, produces a few hundred watches a year and also designs mechanical objets such as cufflinks. The brand is a member of the Fondation de la Haute Horlogerie and continues to refine its three core collections: Logical One, Insight and C.

name: Samsung (Galaxy Watch)
tagline: Android's leading smartwatch, famous for its rotating bezel
summary: Samsung Electronics has made smartwatches since the 2013 Galaxy Gear, and its Galaxy Watch line is the leading watch for Android users. Recent models run Wear OS, and the line includes the rotating-bezel Classic and the titanium Galaxy Watch Ultra.
history:
Samsung Electronics, founded in 1969 as part of the Samsung group started by Lee Byung-chul, launched its first smartwatch, the Galaxy Gear, in 2013 alongside the Galaxy Note 3. Early Gear models used Android and then Samsung's own Tizen system, and the 2015 Gear S2 introduced a rotating bezel for navigating the round screen, a feature that became a hallmark.

The line was renamed Galaxy Watch in 2018, and in 2021 Samsung and Google merged their efforts into the Wear OS platform, with the Galaxy Watch4 as the first Samsung watch to run it. Samsung added body-composition analysis, ECG and blood-pressure features (in supported markets), and sleep coaching.

The 2024 Galaxy Watch Ultra introduced a titanium cushion-shaped case with 10 ATM water resistance aimed at outdoor athletes. The current range includes the Galaxy Watch9, the Galaxy Watch8 Classic with its rotating bezel, and the Galaxy Watch Ultra2, sold alongside Samsung's Galaxy phones from its headquarters in Suwon, South Korea. Galaxy Watches are designed to work best with Samsung's Galaxy phones, and features such as ECG and blood-pressure monitoring depend on regional approvals. The line is one of the best-selling smartwatches in the world outside the Apple ecosystem.

name: Sea-Gull (Tianjin Seagull)
tagline: China's pioneering movement maker, from the 1963 air force chronograph to tourbillons
summary: Tianjin Seagull is China's oldest and most important mechanical watchmaker and one of the world's largest producers of mechanical movements. Famous for the 1963 aviation chronograph reissue, it also makes tourbillons, minute repeaters and other high complications at comparatively low prices.
history:
Seagull began in January 1955 as the state-run Tianjin Watch Factory, started by four craftsmen, and that year produced the Wuxing (Five Star), considered China's first domestically made mechanical wristwatch. In 1963 the factory developed the D304, a manually wound chronograph built for the Chinese Air Force and regarded as China's first aviation chronograph.

Through the planned-economy decades the factory produced millions of watches and the Chinese standard movement. It gained national company status in 1990 and in 1992 became Tianjin Seagull Corporation. After a brief push into quartz, it returned to mechanical watchmaking exclusively in 1997, and it listed on the stock market in 2000. Its movements, including the ST19 chronograph calibre descended from Swiss Venus tooling, have been used by many brands worldwide.

Seagull has since moved into haute horlogerie, presenting the ST9250 in 2009, combining a tourbillon, minute repeater and perpetual calendar, and developing multi-axis and ultra-thin tourbillons. In 2010 it moved to new facilities near Tianjin airport. The 1963 chronograph, reissued in modern form and updated in 2023 for its 60th anniversary, remains its best-known watch abroad, and in 2025 it launched a global direct-to-consumer website.

name: Seiko
tagline: Japan's watchmaking giant, from the first quartz watch to cult-favorite divers
summary: Seiko is Japan's most famous watch brand and one of the few truly vertically integrated manufacturers in the world, making everything from hairsprings to quartz crystals in-house. It changed the industry forever with the 1969 Astron, the world's first quartz wristwatch, and remains a benchmark for value-driven mechanical watches.
history:
Seiko traces its roots to 1881, when 21-year-old Kintaro Hattori opened a watch and clock shop, K. Hattori, in Tokyo's Ginza district. In 1892 he founded the Seikosha factory to produce wall clocks, and in 1913 it made the Laurel, Japan's first wristwatch. The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 destroyed the factory, but Hattori rebuilt, and in 1924 the first watches bearing the Seiko name appeared.

The post-war decades turned Seiko into a technical powerhouse. Internal competition between its Suwa Seikosha and Daini Seikosha factories produced Grand Seiko (1960), King Seiko (1961) and Japan's first diver's watch (1965). Seiko timed the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and, in 1969, launched the Quartz Astron, the world's first quartz wristwatch, along with one of the first automatic chronographs, the 6139.

Quartz technology, which Seiko chose not to lock behind patents, reshaped the global industry and helped trigger the 'quartz crisis' that devastated Swiss watchmaking in the 1970s and 80s. Seiko continued innovating with Kinetic (1988), Spring Drive (1999) and the Astron GPS Solar (2012).

Today Seiko Watch Corporation is part of Seiko Group Corporation, still led by the Hattori family. Its range stretches from the affordable Seiko 5 Sports to Prospex divers, Presage dress watches and Astron, while Grand Seiko was spun off as an independent brand in 2017.

name: Serica
tagline: Parisian instrument watches with enamel dials and COSC chronometer movements
summary: Serica is a Paris-based independent brand founded in 2019 by Jérôme Burgert and Gabriel Vachette. It makes compact, Swiss-made, COSC-certified 'instrument' watches, including field, dive and GMT chronometers and the Parade dress watch, known for enamel-look dials, lyre lugs and superb mesh bracelets.
history:
Serica was founded in Paris in 2019 by Jérôme Burgert and Gabriel Vachette with the aim of creating mechanical watches that combine robustness and technical sophistication with a singular, refined aesthetic. Rather than chasing trends, the founders conceived each collection as a precise instrument for a specific use, drawing on mid-century military, diving and aviation references while applying a distinctly French sense of proportion and finish.

The brand's early field and dive watches established its look: compact cases of 38-39mm, alternating polished and satin surfaces, lyre-shaped lugs, glossy black enamel-style dials with domed luminous indices, and double-domed sapphire crystals. Serica paid unusual attention to bracelets, offering woven 'Vesper' mesh, Bonklip-style and 'Expedition' bracelets with integrated end links. Its watches use Swiss-made Soprod movements, and in 2023 Serica achieved official COSC chronometer certification across its collections, an uncommon distinction at its price point.

The range now includes the Chronomètre Étanche field watches (refs. 6190 and 7505), the Chronomètre de Plongée divers (refs. 5303 and 5330) rated to 300m, the Chronomètre de Voyage GMT (ref. 8315) with a bi-colour ceramic bezel, and, since 2024, the Parade (ref. 1174), a slim stadium-shaped dress watch with a guilloché and sunburst dial. In 2025 Serica added new steel bracelets and limited editions. The company remains independent, selling direct and through its boutique on Rue de Turenne in Paris's Marais district.

name: Shinola
tagline: Detroit-built quartz and automatic watches that helped revive 'Made in America' cool
summary: Shinola is a Detroit-based lifestyle brand founded in 2011 by Fossil co-founder Tom Kartsotis's investment firm, best known for watches assembled in the city's Argonaut Building. Its Runwell, Canfield and Monster collections made it the most visible American watch assembler of the 2010s.
history:
Shinola was created in 2011 by Bedrock Manufacturing, the Texas investment firm of Fossil co-founder Tom Kartsotis. The company bought the name of a defunct American shoe-polish brand, remembered from the phrase 'you don't know shit from Shinola', and chose Detroit, a city struggling after the collapse of its manufacturing economy, as its home. A watch-assembly plant was built inside the College for Creative Studies' Argonaut Building, with Swiss movement specialist Ronda helping to train local workers.

The first watch, the Runwell, launched in 2013 and its limited edition sold out quickly. Shinola expanded rapidly into leather goods, bicycles, audio, jewelry and a hotel on Woodward Avenue, becoming a symbol of Detroit's revival. In 2016 the US Federal Trade Commission told the company to stop using the slogan 'Where American is Made', since many components were imported; Shinola now says its watches are 'Built in Detroit'.

Over time the company added its own Argonite quartz calibres assembled in-house, the Canfield sport line and automatic divers such as the Monster. By 2025 Shinola said it had assembled more than one million watches in Detroit, and after the US imposed steep tariffs on Swiss imports it ran a full-page newspaper ad inviting Swiss watchmakers to manufacture in Detroit.

name: Simon Brette
tagline: A French engineer's marine-chronometer-inspired debut from Geneva
summary: Simon Brette is a Geneva-based independent founded in 2021 by a French engineer who previously designed movements at Chronode, MCT and MB&F. His Chronomètre Artisans, with a hand-engraved red-gold dial and slow 2.5Hz beat, was launched through a collector subscription edition.
history:
Simon Brette, the son of a carpenter, trained as an engineer and worked as a technical designer and movement constructor at Chronode, MCT and MB&F, contributing to some of the most unconventional mechanisms of the 2010s. In 2021 he set up his own brand in Geneva.

His first watch, the Chronomètre Artisans, was presented in 2023. Drawing on marine chronometers, its proprietary calibre SBCA beats at a slow 2.5Hz and runs for 72 hours on twin barrels. The dial combines a 5N red-gold base hand-engraved with a 'dragon scale' motif, translucent sapphire plates for the minutes and seconds, and an observatory-style hour hand inspired by English watchmaker Derek Pratt.

To fund development, Brette offered a Subscription Edition of just 12 pieces in zirconium to early backers, which sold out at around CHF 50,000 each before a regular production edition in traditional case metals followed. The debut was widely praised as one of the most accomplished first watches by a young independent. He continues to develop the brand from Geneva with a small team, favouring traditional hand-engraving and finishing. Case, dial and movement are all his own designs.
